## The shape

A script emits a machine-readable line that callers grep, with a human-readable line directly above it:

```
No affected workspaces (and no repo-wide invariant guard matched the changed paths).
AFFECTED_TESTS_RESULT status=passed tasks=0 failed=0 … reason=no-affected-workspaces
```

The guard for "the marker is emitted on every exit path" was written as a regex over the **source text** of `scripts/affected-tests.mjs`, pinning both lines. Twice, a pure copy edit to the prose — a trailing `.` added to `…none declare a 'test' script.`, then a clarifying tail added to `No affected workspaces` — turned the fleet's green gate red. Nothing functional changed either time; the marker was emitted correctly throughout.

Both times the fix loosened *that one* assertion and wrote a comment explaining why. Neither time did the sibling two feet away get the same treatment. When the class was finally reviewed, the same file still had **two** exact-prose pins armed (`'\nAll affected tests passed.'` and `non-quarantined task(s) failed:`) — a third and fourth recurrence already queued.

> A fix applied to the instance instead of the class does not survive contact with the next edit. The tell that you are looking at a class is that the file **already contains a comment explaining the same lesson**.

## Blind spot 1 — contract vs decoration

A source-text regex cannot distinguish the **contract** (the marker a caller greps) from the **decoration** (the prose above it). So every wording edit is a coin flip against a shared gate.

The cost is asymmetric and lands on a third party: the editor sees green locally if they skip the suite, and the gate reds for everyone else.

> ⚠ This is the counterpoint to [negative assertions rot silently](/internal/docs/agent-insights/negative-assertions-rot-silently), which correctly notes that a POSITIVE literal-pinned assertion "fails loudly when the string is reworded, forcing you to look at it". True — but on a shared gate, *loudly* means "in someone else's run, about a change that is not theirs". Loud is a virtue only when the failure is informative; here it is pure noise, because the pinned bytes were never the contract.

## Blind spot 2 — reachability (the worse one)

A source-text assertion **passes identically whether the code it pins runs or is dead.** It asserts presence, not execution.

That is not hypothetical. In this exact file's subject, an early `process.exit(0)` sat 46 lines above the `REPO_WIDE_INVARIANT_GUARDS` loop, making every repo-wide guard unreachable for any change routing to no workspace — presenting as a healthy `AFFECTED_TESTS_RESULT status=passed tasks=0`. A source-shape guard would have stayed green through the entire bug, because the code it pinned was still *there*.

Executing the path closes both holes at once: prose becomes free to change, and a path that stops being reachable fails loudly.

## The decision procedure

Before reaching for a source-text regex, ask **"is this path cheap to DRIVE?"** — a question that is rarely asked, because the phrase "a full run needs a real repo tree and real test children" is usually true of the *expensive* path and gets generalised to all of them.

Here it was false for exactly the paths that kept breaking. All three early-exit paths `exit(0)` **before** spawning any test child:

| path | how to reach it | cost |
|---|---|---|
| `reason=no-affected-workspaces` | an unrouted path + `--exclude` every workspace in play | — |
| `reason=no-test-script` | a routed path + `--exclude` every workspace in play | — |
| `status=dry-run` | `--dry` | — |
| | **all three combined** | **0.45s** |

The assertions that keep breaking are often the cheapest ones to execute, because "emits X and exits early" is exactly the kind of path that has no expensive setup.

Keep source-shape assertions only where driving the path is genuinely expensive (here: a real *failing* run needs real vitest children), and pin **code tokens** there — `resultLine('failed')`, `process.exit(1)` — never wording.

## Derive the fixture inputs; do not hardcode them

Reaching the empty-task exits requires excluding every workspace that would contribute a task. Today all 17 repo-wide guards live in `@papercusp/operator-core`, so `--exclude @papercusp/operator-core` works — and hardcoding that would reintroduce a staleness trap one level up from the prose pins being removed.

Instead, read the script's own `--dry` task list and exclude what it names:

```ts
function workspacesInPlay(paths: string): string[] {
  const { stdout } = runAffected(['--changed-paths', paths, '--dry']);
  const names = new Set<string>();
  for (const line of stdout.split('\n')) {
    const m = /^\s+-\s+(\S+)\s+::\s+\S+$/.exec(line);
    if (m) names.add(m[1]);
  }
  return [...names];
}
```

When an expectation *is* setup-dependent, say so **in the failure message**, so a stale fixture does not read as a broken contract:

```ts
expect(
  fields.reason,
  `reached a different early-exit path than intended — either the marker contract changed, or this probe's --changed-paths/--exclude inputs went stale. Output:\n${stdout}`,
).toBe(c.reason);
```

## Do NOT build the obvious "guard for the guard" — measured

The tempting class fix is a lint banning human prose inside source-text assertions. **Measure the population before encoding that rule.** Across this repo:

| | count |
|---|---|
| test files reading a file | 535 |
| binding a var to `readFileSync` | 240 |
| with ≥1 assertion pinning 3+ consecutive prose words | **22** |
| such assertions | **57** |

Bounded — but reading the hits, *most pin prose that genuinely IS the contract*: a generated doc's `## heading`, a persona's rule sentence, a projected prompt's literal body. A lint on the pattern would fire mostly on **correct** assertions and would pressure people to loosen tests that should stay tight.

The heuristic cannot separate contract-prose from decoration-prose — which is the same distinction the broken assertions could not make. A guard built on it inherits the defect it was meant to police.

> Also: that probe **under-counted** its own target file (it missed the hyphenated `non-quarantined task(s) failed:`). A pattern census is a floor, not a total — state the filter whenever you report one.

## Proving it falsifiable without dirtying the shared tree

A guard that has never failed is a guard you have not tested — but the obvious probe is unsafe here. git-sync sweeps the **whole** working tree every few minutes, so a mutation held in place for the length of a suite run can be **committed even when nothing goes wrong and no handler fails**. A `trap` does not fix that; it is a different race.

The script resolves its own root (`resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..')`), so a bare `/tmp` copy resolves the wrong root and cannot run. Build a scratch root of **symlinks** instead — every repo entry linked, one real copy of the file under test — plus a test-only env seam pointing at it:

```ts
const AFFECTED_TESTS = process.env.PAPERCUSP_AFFECTED_TESTS_SCRIPT
  ? resolve(process.env.PAPERCUSP_AFFECTED_TESTS_SCRIPT)
  : resolve(REPO_ROOT, 'scripts/affected-tests.mjs');
```

Then prove all three directions — and note that the *passing* row is the one that matters:

| mutation | expected | observed |
|---|---|---|
| prose completely rewritten | **PASS** | ✅ 8/8 green |
| marker emission deleted | FAIL | ✅ `expected exactly one marker line, got: []` |
| `reason=` token renamed | FAIL | ✅ `expected 'nothing-selected' to be 'no-affected-workspaces'` |

A falsifiability probe that only demonstrates failures has not shown the guard is *well-targeted* — only that it is sensitive. The row proving the guard **ignores** the change class that used to break it is what shows the fix actually landed.

## When a source-text assertion is still right

- The path is genuinely expensive to execute (needs real test children, a real network, a real desktop).
- The thing being asserted is a **source-order / structural** property that execution cannot observe — e.g. "the failure announcement and `process.exit(1)` are inseparable", which is a claim about the code's shape, not about any one run.
- The prose **is** the contract (a generated doc's heading, a persona rule) — then pin it exactly, and expect it to fail loudly on a reword, because that is the point.
